title: What’s gone wrong with welfare?
gist: Paul Gregg argues Britain's welfare system has malfunctioned over the last decade: out-of-work claimants are up roughly 1.5-2 million since 2016 despite higher employment, because post-2016 austerity and a binary Universal Credit design replaced a 1996-2016 mix of conditionality, work incentives, coaching and job programmes. Labour's reforms so far look cost-saving rather than system-redesigning.

insights.claim: In May 2026, 8.4 million people were in families receiving Universal Credit, of whom 5.2 million were out of work.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Sizes the fiscal and labour-supply burden of the UK welfare caseload.

insights.claim: Claims for health-related out-of-work benefits (ESA or UC-Health) have risen by about a million since 2016-17 to 3.5 million.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Incapacity claims are the main driver of welfare spending growth and labour-force inactivity.

insights.claim: Total out-of-work claimants in the UK are up roughly 1.5 to just over 2 million since 2016, depending on how the claimant-count methodology change is treated.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Large structural rise in dependency complicates the fiscal outlook and labour supply.

insights.claim: Claimant count rose 900,000 since mid-2016 to 1.7 million, mostly from the Universal Credit methodology change, but is up 170,000 since 2022.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Headline claimant-count comparisons across the UC transition overstate the underlying rise; the post-2022 increase is the real signal.

insights.claim: The rise in out-of-work claims occurred while working-age employment rose by over 2 million since mid-2016, which makes the trend surprising rather than cyclical.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Claims are decoupled from the employment cycle, pointing to system design rather than demand weakness.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: State Pension Age rises since 2018 added nearly 100,000 to incapacity benefit claims, a minor part of the overall rise.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Demographic and policy-mechanical factors explain only a small share of the increase.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: Employment of 16-24-year-olds not in full-time education fell from just under 77 per cent before the pandemic to 68 per cent, almost all between June 2022 and June 2024.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: A sharp youth employment slump feeds later inactivity and benefit claims.

insights.claim: The single-parent employment rate rose from 44 to almost 70 per cent between 1996 and December 2019, then fell back to 64 per cent, with consequences for child poverty.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: The reversal erodes what was the signature welfare-to-work success and raises child poverty pressure.

insights.claim: In January 2024 DWP data showed nearly 475,000 Searching for Work claimants (almost one in three) had claimed for six or more months and 320,000 (one in five) for at least 12 months; DWP has since stopped regularly publishing this data.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Long-term unemployment is likely higher now, and the loss of published data reduces transparency.

insights.claim: The fall-off in entry-level retail and hospitality jobs for the young since 2022 has had major adverse effects on the youth labour market.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Weak entry-level hiring in consumer sectors links sector labour demand to youth benefit claims.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: Overlaps between groups are significant: young adults are a disproportionate share of the long-term unemployed, about a fifth of unemployed 18-24s were unemployed 12+ months over two years (peaking above a quarter in mid-2025), and rising single-parent worklessness partly reflects ill-health.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Policy targeting by group understates compounding health and youth problems.

insights.claim: Part of the paradox is compositional: employment rose among groups less likely to claim if out of work (partnered mothers up nearly 10 points 2002-2021; 50-64 employment from 57 per cent in 1995 to 72 per cent in 2026), while it fell among groups more likely to claim.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Headline employment gains can mask deterioration among high-claim-risk groups.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

themes.theme: What worked 1996-2016 and what replaced it

insights.claim: From 1996 to 2016, across Labour and Conservative-led governments, four strategies reduced welfare reliance: conditionality, strong in-work financial incentives (tax credits from 1999), work coaches, and job placements and employment support such as the New Deals and the Future Jobs Fund.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Gives a reusable package for judging whether current reform proposals are likely to work.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: In the same period the share of unemployed out of work for over 12 months fell from just under 39 per cent in the mid-1990s to 27 per cent by 2016, and health-benefit claims drifted down.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Shows that the post-2016 rise is a reversal of a two-decade improvement.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: Universal Credit's rollout coincided with austerity cuts, so the general work allowance was restricted to those with children or a health-related incapacity claim, weakening work incentives for others, especially renters without children.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Fiscal constraint at launch compromised incentive design, with lasting labour-supply effects.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: Conditionality was ramped up under the Intensive Work Search Regime and sanctioning exploded, while job-search support shrank to monitoring and sanctions rather than practical help.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: The cheap, sanction-based approach failed to cut claims.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: In 2024-25 someone out of work due to ill health received more than twice as much as someone unemployed, and incapacity benefits carry no job-search rules, making the system binary for people without children.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Strong financial pull toward incapacity claims explains drift of an ageing, increasingly impaired population into them.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: The low-cost reliance on conditionality and sanctions has clearly failed, and the binary welfare design pushes an ageing, increasingly impaired population to claim incapacity benefits rather than work limited hours with in-work top-ups.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Core diagnosis implies reform should add an intermediate, supported part-time work option.
insights.quote: But this low-cost strategy of largely relying on conditionality and sanctions to get unemployed claimants into work has clearly failed
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: Employment programmes are time-limited and small: Kickstart ended in 2022, successful mental-health programmes (Individual Placement and Support, Connect to Work, WorkWell) have been small scale, and the UK spends much less on employment programmes than European peers.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Scaling proven mental-health employment support is a candidate for future spending.
insights.locator: Where did it all go wrong?

insights.claim: There was surprisingly little welfare reform after 2016, and Labour in opposition developed no whole-system critique, unlike Gordon Brown before 1997 or Iain Duncan Smith before 2010.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Reform capacity is weaker than past eras, raising odds of piecemeal, savings-led change.

insights.claim: Labour's 2025 Green Paper proposed abolishing the Work Capability Assessment in favour of PIP alone, plus a lower-tier UC rate, which would create room for limited working as an explicit goal; its status is unclear and no extra conditionality, job coaches or supports have been funded.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Without funded support the proposed third option is unlikely to cut claims.

insights.claim: Youth measures have been reintroduced: practical engagement, a hiring subsidy at six months of unemployment, job guarantee pilots and placements, with an Alan Milburn review looking at preventing direct moves from education to incapacity benefits.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Signals a possible youth welfare and skills overhaul that may create new employer subsidy flows.

insights.claim: Labour's welfare delivery record is poor: planned big cuts to PIP eligibility were torpedoed by a backbench rebellion, and the Timms-led PIP review need not cut spending relative to fast-growing forecasts.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Planned welfare savings are politically fragile, which is a fiscal risk for UK budget forecasts.

insights.claim: The 2025 reforms and entitlement cuts appear primarily aimed at saving money rather than fixing the failing system design.
insights.speaker: Paul Gregg
insights.so_what: Savings-led reform risks neither fixing claims growth nor delivering durable fiscal savings.
insights.quote: it’s hard to escape the feeling that the 2025 reforms and the cuts to entitlements are primarily just trying to save money
